per_question.question: According to the HEDNA report referenced in the Coventry Planning Document, what is the total employment land need for Coventry from 2021 to 2041 and from 2021 to 2050?
per_question.answer:
The total employment land need for Coventry from 2021 to 2041 is 156.1 hectares (HEDNA Executive Summary, Table 2.1). 
The total employment land need for Coventry from 2021 to 2050 is 224.0 hectares (HEDNA Executive Summary, Table 2.2).

It has been prepared by a consultancy team which includes Iceni Projects, Cambridge Econometrics, MDS Transmodal and Justin Gardner Consulting (JGC). 1.2 The HEDNA evidence shows that Coventry and Warwickshire can be regarded as a coherent housing market area and ‘best fit’ functional economic market area, albeit that there are differences in the economic characteristics between the north and south of the area, with Coventry and the north of the area more focused towards manufacturing, warehousing and logistics; with South Warwickshire having a more service-orientated economy and higher housing costs. Overlaps are identified with other areas, in particular in North Warwickshire and Stratford-on-Avon districts towards Birmingham; between Rugby and Northamptonshire; and across the A5 with Hinckley and Bosworth. ECONOMY AND EMPLOYMENT LAND REQUIREMENTS Key Economic Characteristics 2.1 Coventry and Warwickshire is a £26 billion economy, accounting for 19% of West Midlands GVA. Immediately prior to the Covid-19 pandemic, growth in GVA was slightly out-performing regional and national trends reflecting stronger performance of the sub-regional economy post 2013. Total employment in 2019 across Coventry and Warwickshire is estimated at 526,900 jobs. Whilst more recent data is not available at the local level, the regional evidence suggests total employment has now returned to the pre-Covid position. The strongest economic performance in recent years has been in Coventry and South Warwickshire and these are the areas which have a stronger skills profile, with higher representation of those with degree-level skills, and a higher business density. 2.2 Economic participation rate in the sub-region (79.3%) is marginally above the national rate (78.8%) but considerably stronger than the region (77.5%). It is lower in Coventry than other areas. The onset of Covid-19 led to an increase in unemployment, and whilst levels have since fallen there remains a particular concentration of unemployed persons in Coventry. 2.3 Manufacturing is the largest sector in employment terms, accommodating 58,000 jobs, and is both a significant employment and an important contributor to wealth creation within the economy. Other sectors which are strongly represented include those associated with warehousing and logistics, which accommodates alongst 48,000 jobs; together with education, with the universities in particular 2 being

to improve connectivity. Issue 6 – Does the Local Plan make adequate and appropriate provisions to meet employment development needs? 176. Coventry’s economic base has shifted from a predominance of manufacturing over recent decades. Today the majority of jobs are in healthcare and education. These trends have meant changing needs in terms of employment land and premises. The growth in employment and diversification is predicted to continue throughout the Plan period. The Council’s employment land review64 has considered recent take up rates based on annualised averages and actual completions. It has also had regard to projected employment growth, market signals and the City’s relationship to employment land on its boundary. It recommends that there is a gross employment land requirement of around 215 ha over the Plan period, which includes a 58 ha 5 year supply margin. In terms of the Coventry and Warwickshire LEP area, the recent employment land use study conducted for the wider area recommends that between 500 and 660 ha of employment land is required up to 2031. 177. Approximately 64 ha of employment land in Coventry is identified in the SHLAA as potentially suitable for housing, whilst since the start of the Plan period around 90 ha of employment land has been granted planning permission or developed for employment uses. Thus when considering employment growth needs as a whole, adding this additional 154 ha to the 215 ha identified, the City’s employment land requirement is 369 ha. There is thus an identified shortfall. This is planned to be provided within Coventry and also in Warwickshire but adjacent to the City boundary - principally at Ansty Park, Ryton Park and Coventry Gateway which are being actively promoted by neighbouring Councils. The proposed redistribution has been agreed as part of the Coventry and Warwickshire Employment Land MOU65. MM22 would set out the land supply position and agreed redistribution across the sub-region more clearly. 178. Coventry’s employment land supply is approximately 146.5 ha within or immediately adjacent to the City boundary. However, if recent completions are taken into account this figure falls to approximately 101 ha. With signs of strong growth in the demand for new employment land around Coventry and Warwickshire, the Council’s evidence base points to the need to boost supply in the medium to longer term. Immediate supply within the area is identified as being sufficient but longer term supply is flagged as being problematic due to a reliance on a number of large sites and constraints imposed by Green Belt policy. As such, the Council seeks to allocate additional land for employment development within the Green Belt as well as supporting its Warwickshire 64 G L Hearn Employment Land Review 2015: Examination Document LP30 65 Coventry & Warwickshire Employment Land MOU: Examination Document LP209 Coventry City Council Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017 42 neighbours’ intentions to allocate additional sites adjacent to the City boundary within the wider Green Belt. 179. per_question.question: According to national decision-making policy E2, what factors should be considered when a development proposal is required to demonstrate whether an unmet need exists, including compliance with policy S5?
per_question.answer:
According to national decision-making policy E2, when a development proposal is required to demonstrate whether an unmet need exists, including compliance with policy S5, consideration should be given to whether market signals indicate an undersupply of specific types of land or premises (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, National decision-making policies E2, 2a). 
This includes taking into account the anticipated catchment area for the type of development proposed, the changing needs of different sectors, and the availability of existing land and buildings (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, National decision-making policies E2, 2a). 
Consideration should also be given to whether a development proposal's specific locational requirements are met by existing allocations in the development plan (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, National decision-making policies E2, 2b). 
This includes situations where existing businesses plan to expand or improve their premises, or clusters or networks of businesses need to grow (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, National decision-making policies E2, 2bi). 
It also includes situations where the availability of infrastructure makes certain locations particularly important (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, National decision-making policies E2, 2bii). 
Proposals that would meet a local, regional or national need for the provision of new, expanded or upgraded facilities that would result in more efficient, reliable or resilient supply chains should also be considered (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, National decision-making policies E2, 2biii).

per_question.question: According to policy GB6, under what circumstances can inappropriate development in the Green Belt be approved?
per_question.answer:
Inappropriate development in the Green Belt can be approved under policy GB6 if very special circumstances exist (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, GB6.2). 
Such circumstances will not exist unless the potential harm to the Green Belt by reason of inappropriateness and any other harm resulting from the proposed development is clearly outweighed by other considerations (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, GB6.2). 
In making this assessment, substantial weight should be given to the harm to the Green Belt which would be caused, including harm to its openness (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, GB6.2).

per_question.question: According to the Green Belt assessment conducted in 2007 and the study in 2015, which parts of the Eastern Green site were identified as having potential for development and why?
per_question.answer:
The Green Belt assessment conducted in 2007 identified the southern part of the Eastern Green site as having potential for development (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 136). The study conducted in 2015 also scored the area lower in recognition of the urbanising features towards the north east of the site around the golf course and hotel (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report, paragraph 136). The area assessed includes the Green Belt land to the west of Pickford Green Lane south of the A45 up to the boundary with Solihull, which is rolling farmland with some farms and other residential buildings (Coventry Green Belt Review, section 4.2.2). The southern part of the site was considered suitable due to its landform, which includes a broad plateau to the immediate north of Eastern Green that then slopes down to the first of the two streams (Coventry Green Belt Review, section 4.2.1). If careful boundaries were drawn to the plateau area, the visual impact of its development from the north and west would be relatively minimal (Coventry Green Belt Review, section 4.2.3).

References:
- Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report — paragraph 136
- Coventry Green Belt Review — sections 4.2.1, 4.2.2, 4.2.3

per_question.question: According to policy E1 in the National Planning Policy, what should development plans do to support business investment and employment?
per_question.answer:
To support business investment and employment, development plans should, at the most appropriate level, set out a clear economic vision and strategy, address potential barriers to investment, and allocate sites to implement the economic vision and strategy (National Planning Policy, Policy E1). 
Development plans should take a positive, proactive and realistic approach to encouraging sustainable economic growth in both urban and rural areas, having regard to the Industrial Strategy and any relevant strategic and local strategies for economic development and regeneration (National Planning Policy, Policy E1a). 
They should also take into account both local business needs and wider opportunities for economic growth, including priority places for investment in key sectors set out in the Industrial Strategy, and the location of Industrial Strategy Zones and AI Growth Zones (National Planning Policy, Policy E1a). 
Additionally, development plans should seek to address potential barriers to investment, such as inadequate infrastructure, services or housing, or a poor environment (National Planning Policy, Policy E1b). 
Development plans should allocate sites to implement the economic vision and strategy and meet existing and anticipated needs over the plan period, paying particular regard to facilitating development to meet the needs of a modern economy (National Planning Policy, Policy E1c). 
This includes making provision for clusters, networks and sites for knowledge and data-driven, creative or high technology industries, storage and distribution operations, and the expansion or modernisation of other businesses of local, regional or national importance (National Planning Policy, Policy E1c).

References:
- National Planning Policy, Policy E1 
- National Planning Policy, Policy E1a 
- National Planning Policy, Policy E1b 
- National Planning Policy, Policy E1c

per_question.question: According to the Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, what policy approaches are recommended to promote sustainable development as indicated in Table 9?
per_question.answer:
The policy approaches recommended to promote sustainable development as indicated in Table 9 are: 
* New housing growth in the city centre (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 17 of 48).
* New housing growth at higher densities within the existing built up area (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 17 of 48).
* Provision of new employment opportunities within the city centre and major regeneration areas, depending on the type and nature of employment proposed (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 17 of 48).
* Consider limits on types of houses to ensure local needs are met and empty units are not created, and ensure sufficient housing for elderly people to enable larger housing to be freed up for families (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Page 17 of 48).

per_question.question: According to the Supplementary Planning Document, what restrictions are placed on new vehicular access onto Kenilworth Road within the Conservation Area?
per_question.answer:
According to the Supplementary Planning Document, no new vehicular access be provided onto Kenilworth Road and that access from subsidiary roads to the rear of any development shall be provided wherever possible (Kenilworth_Road_control_plan, Section 2.4). The City Council will not grant any further permissions for access across Council owned land onto Kenilworth Road where it has the power to do so (Kenilworth_Road_control_plan, Section 3).

References:
- Kenilworth_Road_control_plan: Kenilworth Road control plan — Section 2.4, Section 3
contexts: Kenilworth Road is one of the most attractive entrances to any city in the country. It has a heavily landscaped and well-wooded character and also includes the ancient Styvechale Common and the more recent War Memorial Park. Development behind the landscaped screen is of a wide variety of types of housing on predominantly large plots. The conservation area was designated in 1967. The following guidelines will be applied in the determination of planning applications within the Conservation Area 1. New development or redevelopment entailing the intensification of land use along Kenilworth Road will not generally be permitted. 2. In those very exceptional cases where development or redevelopment is considered to be acceptable, the following criteria will be taken into account; 2.1 that such development or redevelopment shall not be so located as to necessitate the removal of or cause damage to trees or associated ground cover; 2.2 that such development or redevelopment be set at such distance from the existing spinneys as to ensure that it is screened from Kenilworth Road; 2.3 that the height of any development or redevelopment be restricted to two storey (excluding accommodation within the roof space); 2.4 that no new vehicular access be provided onto Kenilworth Road and that access from subsidiary roads to the rear of any development shall be provided wherever possible; 2.5 that existing drives be not utilised to provide access to more than one additional dwelling; 2.6 that a comprehensive landscaping scheme be submitted as part of any detailed application for planning permission; 2.7 that screen fences, etc, be finished in natural colours; and 2.8 that adequate foul and surface water drainage facilities must exist. 3. The City Council, where it has powers so to do, will not grant any further permissions for access across Council owned land onto Kenilworth Road.

The following paragraphs within Section 16 of the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) set out the local authorities statutory requirements when putting together a local plan: 3 190. Plans should set out a positive strategy for the conservation and enjoyment of the historic environment, including heritage assets most at risk through neglect, decay or other threats. This strategy should take into account: (a) the desirability of sustaining and enhancing the significance of heritage assets, and putting them to viable uses consistent with their conservation; (b) the wider social, cultural, economic and environmental benefits that conservation of the historic environment can bring; (c) the desirability of new development making a positive contribution to local character and distinctiveness; and (d) opportunities to draw on the contribution made by the historic environment to the character of a place. 191. When considering the designation of conservation areas, local planning authorities should ensure that an area justifies such status because of its special architectural or historic interest, and that the concept of conservation is not devalued through the designation of areas that lack special interest. 195. Regionally Important Geological Sites (RIGS) Non-statutory sites that are important places for geology, geomorphology and soils. Registered Common Land A piece of land owned and registered under the 1965 Common Land Act by one person, but over which other people can exercise certain traditional rights, such as allowing their livestock to graze upon it. per_question.question: According to Coventry's latest HELA (November 2024), are any adopted allocations or other identified sites anticipated to deliver housing within the next five years?
per_question.answer:
According to Coventry's latest HELA (November 2024), none of the adopted allocations or other identified sites are currently anticipated to deliver housing within the next five years (Five_Year_Housing_Land_Supply_2025_2029_Position_Statement, paragraph 3.3).

The housing trajectory on 31st December 2024 indicates that identified capacity, which includes adopted allocations and other sites identified in Coventry's latest HELA, is expected to deliver housing in years 6-10 and 11-15, but not within the next five years (Five_Year_Housing_Land_Supply_2025_2029_Position_Statement, Table 2).

Specifically, the total dwellings expected from identified capacity is 7,012, with 0 dwellings expected in years 1-5, 2,278 dwellings in years 6-10, and 4,734 dwellings in years 11-15 (Five_Year_Housing_Land_Supply_2025_2029_Position_Statement, Table 2).

The Council acknowledges that the Plan will not, on its own, deliver the full OAN for market and affordable housing in Coventry. In seeking to meet the OAN for housing, the Council’s ‘Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment’ (SHLAA), based on data for 2014/15 and published in January 201620, identifies capacity for around 25,000 homes. Subsequent to this, the Council has updated the figures to present the latest position as of 1 April 2016. This is shown in MM46 and MM48 and brings the total housing land supply to around 25,372 dwellings. This is comprised as follows - adding completions since 2011 (5,550) to sites with planning permission (5,900) and sites under construction (945) gives a total of 12,395 homes. Added to this, the SHLAA identifies sites capable of accommodating 3,058 dwellings. 53. The SHLAA used the joint methodology that was prepared by the 6 neighbouring authorities comprising the HMA. The process involved a robust assessment of 503 sites which were analysed for their suitability and deliverability. Some of these sites were discounted and some were incorporated into LP and City Centre Area Action Plan site allocations. The remaining 113 sites have been identified as deliverable or developable residential or mixed use opportunities. They comprise approximately 67 ha of gross developable land and are anticipated to provide 3,058 dwellings. I am satisfied that the SHLAA methodology is sound, and that the position, as updated, provides an accurate account of the sites that are either deliverable within five years or developable in later years, in accordance with the NPPF. 54. The remaining components of the housing supply comprise LP site allocations (8,920 dwellings), City Centre Area Action Plan allocations (649 dwellings) and a small site windfall allowance of approximately 350 dwellings. The figure is based on sites comprising less than 5 dwellings. It is considered important to consider such a supply given the approach in the SHLAA to maximise supply within Coventry’s administrative area and to reflect local circumstances which shows a continued contribution of housing completions on smaller sites of less than 5 dwellings. The calculation of the allowance excludes the development of residential gardens. Overall, I am satisfied that the windfall allowance is based on sound evidence and is realistic and achievable. Thus the figure of just over 25,000 dwellings represents a sound assessment of the overall housing land supply over the period of the Plan. per_question.question: According to Annex B: Glossary in this planning document, what are the three main types of affordable housing defined?
per_question.answer:
The three main types of affordable housing defined in Annex B: Glossary are: Social Rent (NPPF, Annex B), Other affordable housing for rent (NPPF, Annex B), and Discounted market sales housing (NPPF, Annex B). 
Social Rent meets specific conditions including rent set in accordance with the government's rent policy for Social Rent, landlord being a registered provider, and provisions to remain at an affordable price for future eligible households (NPPF, Annex B). 
Other affordable housing for rent also meets specific conditions such as rent set in accordance with the government's rent policy for Affordable Rent or at least 20% below local market rents, and the landlord being a registered provider except in Build to Rent schemes (NPPF, Annex B). 
Discounted market sales housing is sold at a discount of at least 20% below local market value, with eligibility determined by local incomes and local house prices (NPPF, Annex B).

per_question.question: According to the Coventry Planning Document, what are the key considerations for potential residential development on Parcel 15b (south of the railway line and west of Cromwell Lane)?
per_question.answer:
Parcel 15b, located south of the railway line and west of Cromwell Lane, is gently sloping open farmland with little tree cover and no recorded areas of ecological importance or major physical constraints (GREEN_BELT_REVIEW_Annex_2, Parcel 15b description). 
The farmhouse at Westwood Farm within Parcel 15b is Grade II Listed (GREEN_BELT_REVIEW_Annex_2, Parcel 15b description). 
The 12-hectare site has potential for residential development, with access from Cromwell Lane (GREEN_BELT_REVIEW_Annex_2, Parcel 15b description). 
This development would be subject to sensitive design considerations, including protecting the setting of the Listed Building (GREEN_BELT_REVIEW_Annex_2, Parcel 15b description). 
Boundary native woodland planting is also required to protect the visual amenities of the Green Belt and enhance its ecological value (GREEN_BELT_REVIEW_Annex_2, Parcel 15b description). 
The site's proximity to the railway station and the facilities of Tile Hill Village makes it a suitable location for sustainable residential development (GREEN_BELT_REVIEW_Annex_2, Parcel 15b description).

per_question.question: According to policy HO4, what requirements must the development plan meet when identifying locations for large scale residential and mixed-use development?
per_question.answer:
According to policy HO4, the development plan should identify suitable locations for large scale development, such as new settlements, new urban quarters or significant extensions to existing settlements (Draft NPPF December 2025, Policy HO4, Section 1). 
These locations should be capable of being supported by the necessary infrastructure and facilities at appropriate points in the development’s delivery (Draft NPPF December 2025, Policy HO4, Section 1a). 
They should also support a sustainable community, with sufficient access to services and employment opportunities within the development itself or in larger towns to which there is good access by sustainable transport modes (Draft NPPF December 2025, Policy HO4, Section 1b). 
Additionally, they should address strategic environmental opportunities and safeguards, including those set out in Local Nature Recovery Strategies (Draft NPPF December 2025, Policy HO4, Section 1c). 
Local plans should identify specific sites, infrastructure and other site-specific requirements for large-scale development (Draft NPPF December 2025, Policy HO4, Section 2). 
This includes setting clear expectations for the quality of places to be created, making a realistic assessment of the likely rates of delivery, and supporting delivery by setting expectations for an appropriate mix of tenures (Draft NPPF December 2025, Policy HO4, Sections 2a, 2b, and 2c).

per_question.question: According to the Coventry City Council Authority Monitoring Report 2023/24, what is the annual requirement for new affordable homes established in the Local Plan, and which Local Plan policy sets the threshold for affordable housing provision?
per_question.answer:
The annual requirement for new affordable homes established in the Local Plan is around 348 per year (Authority Monitoring Report 2020/21, paragraph 3.14). 
The Local Plan policy that sets the threshold for affordable housing provision is Policy H6 (Authority Monitoring Report 2020/21, paragraph 3.16). 
Policy H6 states that new residential schemes of 25 dwellings or more, or more than 1 ha, will be expected to provide 25% of all dwellings as affordable homes (Authority Monitoring Report 2020/21, Policy H6).

per_question.question: According to the standard method outlined in the document, how is the baseline for local housing need calculated?
per_question.answer:
The baseline for local housing need is calculated as 0.8% of the existing housing stock for the area (NPPF, Annex D, paragraph 3). The existing housing stock is determined using the Dwelling Stock Estimates data published annually (NPPF, Annex D, paragraph 3).

For example, Coventry's existing housing stock in 2024 was 148,061, so the baseline figure is 1,184 (Authority Monitoring Report 2024/25, Table 12). 
The baseline is then adjusted based on the affordability of the area (NPPF, Annex D, paragraph 4).

per_question.question: According to policy H1 of the Coventry Local Plan (2017), what is the annual housing completion requirement for Coventry City Council from 2017 until 2031?
per_question.answer:
According to policy H1 of the Coventry Local Plan (2017), the annual housing completion requirement for Coventry City Council from 2017 until 2031 is 1,300 homes per annum (Authority Monitoring Report 2017/18, paragraph 2.2). 
Provisions will be made for a minimum of 24,600 additional dwellings between 2011 and 2031, with 1,300 homes per annum required from 2017 to 2031 (Authority Monitoring Report 2023/24, Section 3.1).

per_question.question: According to the Coventry Aquatics Strategy 2014-2024, what has Coventry City Council commissioned regarding the future of the Coventry Sports and Leisure Centre competition pool?
per_question.answer:
Coventry City Council has commissioned a technical options appraisal on the future development of the building and the provision of public sport and leisure (including aquatic) facilities in the city centre (Coventry Aquatics Strategy 2014-2024, Page 4). 
It has considered sixteen options for future city centre sport and public leisure provision: from full and partial refurbishment of the current building; to part closure and part refurbishment; to complete closure; to new provision (Coventry Aquatics Strategy 2014-2024, Page 4).

per_question.question: According to the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) Order 2015, what does an Article 4 direction do?
per_question.answer:
An Article 4 direction is a direction made under Article 4 of the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) Order 2015, which withdraws permitted development rights granted by that Order (NPPF, paragraph as cited in glossary). 
An Article 4 Direction brings under the control of the local planning authority any specified developments normally permitted under the Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 2015 (Coventry Local Plan Appendices, Appendix 4 Glossary).

The Council acknowledges that the Plan will not, on its own, deliver the full OAN for market and affordable housing in Coventry. In seeking to meet the OAN for housing, the Council’s ‘Strategic Housing Land Availability Assessment’ (SHLAA), based on data for 2014/15 and published in January 201620, identifies capacity for around 25,000 homes. Subsequent to this, the Council has updated the figures to present the latest position as of 1 April 2016. This is shown in MM46 and MM48 and brings the total housing land supply to around 25,372 dwellings. This is comprised as follows - adding completions since 2011 (5,550) to sites with planning permission (5,900) and sites under construction (945) gives a total of 12,395 homes. Added to this, the SHLAA identifies sites capable of accommodating 3,058 dwellings. 53. The SHLAA used the joint methodology that was prepared by the 6 neighbouring authorities comprising the HMA. The process involved a robust assessment of 503 sites which were analysed for their suitability and deliverability. Some of these sites were discounted and some were incorporated into LP and City Centre Area Action Plan site allocations. The remaining 113 sites have been identified as deliverable or developable residential or mixed use opportunities. They comprise approximately 67 ha of gross developable land and are anticipated to provide 3,058 dwellings. I am satisfied that the SHLAA methodology is sound, and that the position, as updated, provides an accurate account of the sites that are either deliverable within five years or developable in later years, in accordance with the NPPF. 54. The remaining components of the housing supply comprise LP site allocations (8,920 dwellings), City Centre Area Action Plan allocations (649 dwellings) and a small site windfall allowance of approximately 350 dwellings. The figure is based on sites comprising less than 5 dwellings. It is considered important to consider such a supply given the approach in the SHLAA to maximise supply within Coventry’s administrative area and to reflect local circumstances which shows a continued contribution of housing completions on smaller sites of less than 5 dwellings. The calculation of the allowance excludes the development of residential gardens. Overall, I am satisfied that the windfall allowance is based on sound evidence and is realistic and achievable. Thus the figure of just over 25,000 dwellings represents a sound assessment of the overall housing land supply over the period of the Plan. Meeting the Overall Need for Housing – Addressing the Shortfall 55. The identified housing land supply will clearly not meet the OAN for 42,400 dwellings. As referred to elsewhere in my report, the available evidence, most notably the Council’s SHLAA process, indicates that the allocation of additional sites would not be achievable given the City’s tight administrative boundaries and lack of developable options during the Plan period. per_question.question: According to the 2015 Strategic Flood Risk Assessment referenced in the Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan (CCAAP), what is the current level of surface water flood risk in most of the City Centre?
per_question.answer:
Most of the City Centre has low or very low risk of surface water flooding and there is no currently recognised flood risk as set out in the 2015 Strategic Flood Risk Assessment, Level 1 and Level 2 findings (CCAAP Sustainability Appraisal Report, paragraph 6.20).

per_question.question: According to the Coventry Planning Document, what is the definition of 'Major Development' and which Act should be referenced for its definition unless otherwise stated?
per_question.answer:
According to the Coventry Planning Document, 'Major Development' is defined as 10 or more (gross) residential units or developments of 1,000 sq ms or more of non-residential floorspace (Coventry Planning Document, Contents 50). When referencing this term, consideration should be given to the definition contained within the Town and Country Planning Act unless otherwise stated within the Plan(s) (Coventry Planning Document, Contents 50).

per_question.question: According to policy HO12, what criteria must development proposals for traveller sites meet regarding site design and integration with the community?
per_question.answer:
According to policy HO12, development proposals for traveller sites must be located and designed so that they provide a settled base, enable access to services, promote healthy lifestyles, and avoid isolating the site from the community (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, HO12:1). 
Specifically, the criteria for site design and integration with the community are: 
- Providing a settled base that limits the need for long-distance travelling and potential environmental damage caused by unauthorised encampment (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, HO12:1a).
- Enabling access to education, welfare, and health services, including ensuring that children can attend school on a regular basis (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, HO12:1b).
- Promoting opportunities for healthy lifestyles, such as by providing adequate landscaping and play areas for children, and minimising adverse impacts from local environmental factors on the health and wellbeing of travellers (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, HO12:1c).
- Not enclosing the site such that the site and its occupants appear to be isolated from the rest of the community (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, HO12:1d).

per_question.question: According to policy DM1 in the National Planning Policy, what are the requirements for proposals for major development before submitting a planning application?
per_question.answer:
According to policy DM1 in the National Planning Policy, proposals for major development should be informed by early engagement with neighbours and the local community, as well as with the local planning authority, statutory consultees and other relevant bodies where appropriate, to identify and seek to resolve key planning matters prior to the submission of a planning application (NPPF, DM1:1a). 
Proposals for major development should also be accompanied by a concise planning statement setting out how the proposals are consistent with relevant development plan and national decision-making policies, the outcome of pre-application engagement and the extent to which the proposals have changed in response to this engagement, and the proposed use of any planning obligations to make the proposals acceptable in planning terms (NPPF, DM1:1b). 
The pre-application engagement should be proportionate to the nature of the scheme and those likely to be affected by it (NPPF, DM1:1a).

Looking in turn at the parcels where the Joint Green Belt Study recommended further consideration: Keresley (C19a, C19b, C19c, C19d) These Green Belt parcels in the Parish of Keresley represent the largest area that the Study identified within Coventry. It forms part of the Ancient Arden Landscape, supported by 'Design Guidelines for Development in Coventry's Ancient Arden' which is currently Supplementary Planning Guidance. Within the area of assessment, the northern area is a highly attractive and rural habitat mosaic within the Keresley countryside, with high biodiversity value. The Local Wildlife Sites (SINCs) are Pikehorne Wood, The Alders, Hall Yard Wood and Bunson's Wood, which are all Ancient Woodlands, and the large pool known as Keresley Mere, which also feeds the Hall Brook valley. The woodlands and Keresley Mere are currently privately owned with no public access and represent a particularly fine example of the Ancient Arden countryside, including ancient hedgerows. The woodlands were designated Sites of Importance for Nature Conservation in 1989 and later extended to also include Kerelsey Mere, which in the 1982- 83 Coventry Wildlife Survey, was rated as the best aquatic site in Coventry, recording 71 aquatic species. Hounds Hill and the adjoining Bunson's Wood is the highest part of the city, 500 feet above sea level, with impressive views over Keresley and towards the Coventry three spires in the distance. Archaeological surveys also recognise the importance of this area, particularly in relation to its proximity to the Bronze/Iron Age fortifications at Corley Rocks and Burrow Hill; a scheduled Ancient Monument just beyond the city boundary at 561 feet above sea level. Collectively, this area of Green Belt is considered to be the most sensitive of the Keresley parcels and this has been carefully taken into account in drawing the boundaries of the proposed Green Belt Safeguarded Land and Country Park, linking with the Houldsworth Crescent green space and the Prologis Country Park in Nuneaton & Bedworth Borough Council. Within the area, a biodiversity buffer to help ensure their long-term protection, as recommended by the Coventry Green Belt Ecological Review, is indicated. Existing Public Footpaths have also been protected from development and new footpaths will be required to supplement these and ensure accessibility for passive recreation from the existing surrounding communities. per_question.question: According to Policy CC10 in the City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report (January 2016), what must be submitted and approved by the council before construction or demolition works commence?
per_question.answer:
According to Policy CC10 in the City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report (January 2016), a construction environmental management plan (CEMP) must be submitted to and approved by the council before construction or demolition works commence (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Policy CC10, point 1). The CEMP must specify how the developer will mitigate noise and dust emissions from the works (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Policy CC10, point 1).

per_question.question: Which policies in the Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan (CC1, CC8, CC9, CC11) are identified as requiring a fresh SA/SEA assessment due to substantive changes, according to the March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report?
per_question.answer:
The policies in the Coventry City Centre Area Action Plan that are identified as requiring a fresh SA/SEA assessment due to substantive changes are CC1, CC8, CC9, and CC11 (MOD13_SASEA___CCAAP_Proposed_Modifications_2017, Inspector's letter of January 2017).

CC1 requires a fresh SA/SEA assessment due to substantive changes including a more inclusive reference to integrated University development, public transport system integration, and supporting green and blue infrastructure (MOD13_SASEA___CCAAP_Proposed_Modifications_2017, Inspector's letter of January 2017).
CC8 requires a fresh SA/SEA assessment due to small adjustments in the supporting text to reflect updated flood risk and drainage policies (MOD13_SASEA___CCAAP_Proposed_Modifications_2017, Inspector's letter of January 2017).
CC9 requires a fresh SA/SEA assessment due to small adjustments in the supporting text to reflect updated flood risk and drainage policies (MOD13_SASEA___CCAAP_Proposed_Modifications_2017, Inspector's letter of January 2017).
CC11 requires a fresh SA/SEA assessment due to adjustments to strengthen links to sub-regional and regional public transport and cycle networks (MOD13_SASEA___CCAAP_Proposed_Modifications_2017, Inspector's letter of January 2017).

per_question.question: According to the provided chunk, which types of infrastructure are classified as 'Essential Infrastructure' in flood risk areas?
per_question.answer:
The types of infrastructure classified as 'Essential Infrastructure' in flood risk areas include essential transport infrastructure, essential utility infrastructure, wind turbines, solar farms, hydrogen production facilities, carbon capture, distribution and storage facilities, data centres, and electric vehicle charging stations (Draft_NPPF_December_2025.pdf, Table 2). 
Essential transport infrastructure includes mass evacuation routes which have to cross the area at risk (Draft_NPPF_December_2025.pdf, Table 2). 
Essential utility infrastructure includes infrastructure for electricity supply, including generation, storage and distribution systems, and water treatment works that need to remain operational in times of flood (Draft_NPPF_December_2025.pdf, Table 2). 
Additionally, certain installations requiring hazardous substances consent can be classified as 'Essential Infrastructure' if there is a demonstrable need to locate them in high flood risk areas for specific operational reasons (Draft_NPPF_December_2025.pdf, Table 2).

per_question.question: According to the Health Impact Assessment for the Coventry Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan (2016), what has been the outcome regarding major impacts on health and wellbeing?
per_question.answer:
The Health Impact Assessment for the Coventry Local Plan and City Centre Area Action Plan (2016) has concluded that there are no major impacts on health and wellbeing (Health Impact Assessment: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre AAP, 2016, Section 6.2). 
The assessment found that both documents incorporate aspects that promote health and allow for an increased quality of life for the population (Health Impact Assessment: Coventry Local Plan and City Centre AAP, 2016, Section 6.2).

Improved social cohesion and social capital can benefit health and wellbeing through the provision of community facilities, areas for play, and increased opportunities for walking and cycling. This is incorporated into several policy themes of the Local Plan including health and wellbeing; green environment; design; communities; retail and leisure. Providing suitable shops and centres for people to meet will help to build social capital, as will supporting accessible community facilities such as schools, healthcare and places of worship. The city centre will continue to be the focus for major community and social facilities which will allow accessibility by public transport and will be enabled by the City Centre Area Action Plan. Public transport will be improved according to the both planning policy documents. This will help those without a car, particularly the young, elderly and mobility impaired, to socialise and interact. In turn this will help to reduce social isolation and improve wellbeing. It may also contribute to reducing pollutants from excessive car trips which impact on air quality. Social cohesion is supported by opportunities within green infrastructure which also includes play areas, school grounds, allotment sites and public realm. These areas will need to be well designed to encourage their use and for increased social capital. In larger office developments, it is recommended that there is provision for social interaction. per_question.question: According to policy CC11 Accessibility in the City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report (January 2016), which specific Ring Road junctions are highlighted as priorities for improved connectivity between the city centre and the wider city?
per_question.answer:
According to policy CC11 Accessibility in the City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report (January 2016), the specific Ring Road junctions highlighted as priorities for improved connectivity between the city centre and the wider city are Ring Road Junctions 1, 2, 4, and 5 (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Policy CC11). Development proposals will be required to incorporate improvements to crossing the Ring Road to ensure enhanced connectivity between the city centre and the wider city for pedestrians and cyclists (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Policy CC11). The same priorities are reiterated in the City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017, Policy CC11).

per_question.question: According to the Coventry Green Belt Review, 2007, what recommendation is made regarding the Coundon Court School buildings and their Green Belt status?
per_question.answer:
According to the Coventry Green Belt Review, 2007, it is recommended that the Coundon Court School buildings are taken out of the Green Belt to enable redevelopment for sustainable long-term educational needs, but only to the extent necessary (Coventry Green Belt Review, 2007, paragraph 4.18.5). This should not include the mature trees which are critical in shielding the existing (and potential) buildings from the broader views across the wedge (Coventry Green Belt Review, 2007, paragraph 4.18.5). The Coundon Court School is listed among the locations recommended to be removed from the Green Belt, specifically the built and expansion area (Coventry Green Belt Review, 2007, paragraph 5.7.1).

References:
- Coventry Green Belt Review, 2007 — paragraph 4.18.5
- Coventry Green Belt Review, 2007 — paragraph 5.7.1

per_question.question: What substantive change to Policy HE3 in the Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 requires a fresh SA/SEA assessment?
per_question.answer:
The substantive change to Policy HE3 in the Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 is that it has been developed in partnership with Bluecoats School and the Charterhouse Trust and clarifies the position around how the heritage park will be delivered and how the future expansion of the school can be supported (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Page 51 of 99). It also brings into the policy the specific requirement for a comprehensive Masterplan developed in partnership with both parties alongside the city council and local community (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Page 51 of 99). Due to the substantive changes to the policy, it is considered this represents a significant change to the findings of the SA/SEA report, which would require a fresh SA/SEA assessment (MOD14_SASEA_Final_Report___Local_Plan_Proposed_Modfications_2017, Page 51 of 99).

per_question.question: According to the City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report (January 2016), what are the main benefits of the 'Focused' option for new office development in Coventry city centre?
per_question.answer:
The main benefits of the 'Focused' option for new office development in Coventry city centre are that it would result in office development being located where it is most accessible by public transport and promote rail travel as a principal form of transport for office workers (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 21 of 104). This option would also possibly decrease the levels of air pollution in the city centre and decrease energy consumption through the greater use of renewables (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 21 of 104). Furthermore, it would encourage the promotion of rail travel and help to reduce road congestion, which in turn would help to prevent Coventry being seen as an unattractive location for firms to locate (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Page 22 of 104).

per_question.question: According to the Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report October 2017, what change is made to Policy GB2 regarding land in the Green Belt separated by Coventry City Council and Warwick District Council boundaries?
per_question.answer:
According to the Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report October 2017, Policy GB2 is amended to refer to land in the Green Belt separated by Coventry City Council and Warwick District Council boundaries as 'safeguarded' rather than 'reserved' (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 124). This change clarifies that safeguarded land would be considered as part of any subsequent Plan review if development proposals in Warwick District Council come forward during the Plan period (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 124).

per_question.question: According to policy DP1 in the National Planning Policy, what should development plans do to set out clear design expectations?
per_question.answer:
According to policy DP1 in the National Planning Policy, development plans should set out clear design expectations by: ensuring the vision for the plan reflects the desired design and placemaking outcomes (National Planning Policy, DP1.a); identifying where design guides, design codes and masterplans are necessary to deliver design and placemaking outcomes (National Planning Policy, DP1.b); setting out locally-specific design policies or standards which are necessary to add further detail to the principles in policy DP3 (National Planning Policy, DP1.c); and setting out in what circumstances design review and other design processes will be required (National Planning Policy, DP1.d).

per_question.question: According to policy F6, under what circumstances must the 'exception test' be satisfied for development proposals in flood zones 2, 3a, or 3b?
per_question.answer:
According to policy F6, the 'exception test' must be satisfied for development proposals in flood zones 2, 3a, or 3b in certain circumstances shown in Annex F, table 3, in addition to satisfying the sequential test in policy F5 where applicable (NPPF, Policy F6, 1b). The exception test involves demonstrating that the development would meet all the following criteria: provide wider sustainability benefits to the community that outweigh the flood risk; be safe for its anticipated lifetime in accordance with policy F7; and not increase flood risk elsewhere and, where possible, reduce flood risk overall (NPPF, Policy F6, 1b). 

The exception test does not need to be applied to those forms of development, or in those circumstances, where the sequential test is not required, as set out in policy F5 (NPPF, Policy F6, 2a). The exception test also does not need to be applied where development is proposed on a site allocated in the development plan to which the exception test was applied at the plan-making stage, unless there has been a significant increase in the risk of flooding to the site subsequently, or the nature of the development itself has changed significantly from that which was allocated so as to introduce a more vulnerable use (NPPF, Policy F6, 2b).

per_question.question: According to policy CC1 in the National Planning Policy, what proactive approaches should development plans take to mitigate and adapt to climate change?
per_question.answer:
According to policy CC1 in the National Planning Policy, development plans should take a proactive approach to mitigating climate change and supporting the transition to net zero (NPPF, Policy CC1). They should also take a proactive approach to adapting to climate change, taking into account the implications of extreme weather and long-term climate trends (NPPF, Policy CC1). This includes proposing development patterns through their spatial strategy and allocations which can help contribute to radical reductions in greenhouse gas emissions and avoid increased vulnerability to the effects of climate change (NPPF, Policy CC1(a)). Development plans should address any specific risks from climate change in their proposed allocations for development and necessary adaptations (NPPF, Policy CC1(b)). They should also set local water efficiency standards for new development where justified (NPPF, Policy CC1(c)). Additionally, development plans should identify opportunities for green infrastructure provision and nature-based solutions (NPPF, Policy CC1(d)).

per_question.question: According to the Supplementary Planning Document (SPD) for Tall Buildings and the Three Spires View Management Framework in Coventry, what is a key consideration for any application for tall buildings in and around the city centre?
per_question.answer:
Retaining the views of the city's iconic three spires, and their primacy in the city centre skyline, is a key consideration in any application for tall buildings in and around the city centre (Tall Buildings Design Guide and View Management Framework SPD, paragraph 1.4).

Context (or background) 1.1 The National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) defines Supplementary Planning Documents (SPDs) as ‘documents which add further detail to the policies in the development plan. They can be used to provide further guidance for development on specific sites, or on particular issues…. Supplementary Planning Documents are capable of being a material consideration in planning decisions but are not part of the development plan’. 1.2 The delivery of a Tall Buildings SPD is a provision of Policy CC7 of the City Centre Area Action Plan, adopted by the Council in 2017. Policy CC7 also establishes the protected views of the city’s famous spires. Whilst the document is fairly technical in nature it will help ensure where tall buildings are developed they will integrate well and be positive contributors to the city. 1.3 The SPD has two parts. The first part deals with the information and considerations required for the application for a tall building anywhere within the city, including a clear definition of what a tall building is. It also sets the requirement for a Tall Buildings Statement to be submitted alongside a relevant application, and what should be detailed within it. 1.4 The second part of the SPD uses a range of visual tools to fully articulate the protected views of the three spires, established in the City Centre Area Action Plan, 2017. Each of the 17 views are articulated, and use of 3D imagery enhances this with a clearly defined corridor that must be protected. per_question.question: According to policy TR7, what environmental effects must development proposals for marine ports, airports, and other aviation facilities have?
per_question.answer:
According to policy TR7, development proposals for marine ports, airports, and other aviation facilities must have an acceptable environmental effect in terms of noise, air quality, carbon emissions, the transport network, landscape, visual and marine impacts (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, Policy TR7, subsection d).

per_question.question: According to policy HE5, what minimum resource should be consulted when assessing the significance of heritage assets affected by development proposals?
per_question.answer:
According to policy HE5, the relevant historic environment record should be consulted as a minimum when assessing the significance of heritage assets affected by development proposals (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, HE5:1).

contexts: basis of whether the conservation benefits outweigh the disbenefits of departing from the policies concerned. HE5: Assessing effects on heritage assets 1. Development proposals affecting heritage assets should be accompanied by an assessment of the significance of the assets affected (including any contribution made by their setting) and of the potential effect of the proposal on their significance. The level of detail should be proportionate to the assets’ importance and no more than is necessary to understand the potential effect of the proposal on their significance. The relevant historic environment record should be consulted as a minimum, and appropriate expertise employed where necessary. 2. Assessments of the potential effects of development proposals on heritage assets and their setting should identify whether proposals would be likely to: a. Have a positive effect, which is where a heritage asset would be enhanced, or its significance better revealed; or b. Have no effect on the significance of the asset; or c. Result in harm to the significance of the heritage asset, either from work affecting the asset itself or from development within its setting. The degree of harm should be identified: substantial harm would occur where the development proposal would seriously affect a key element of the asset’s significance; or d. Cause the total loss of the significance of the heritage asset. 3. In making this assessment it is the effect on an asset’s significance rather than the scale of the development which should be considered. 4. Decision makers should be satisfied that this assessment accurately reflects the effects on heritage assets caused by the proposals. 5. Where a development proposal involves, or has the potential to involve, heritage assets with archaeological interest, an appropriate desk-based assessment should be employed and, where necessary, a field evaluation. per_question.question: According to policy TR5, under what circumstances should development proposals for roadside facilities located outside settlements be permitted?
per_question.answer:
According to policy TR5, development proposals for roadside facilities located outside settlements should be permitted if they meet an evidenced need to improve the safety and welfare of road users, or to improve access to electric vehicle charging infrastructure or other alternative fuels, if new or significantly expanded facilities are being proposed (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, TR5:1a). 
This includes the provision of overnight lorry parking facilities to address any local or wider shortages and reduce the risk of parking in locations which lack appropriate facilities or could cause a nuisance (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, TR5:1a). 
Alternatively, development proposals should be permitted if they improve driver welfare and security, support changes in transport technology, or improve environmental impacts, where the proposal is to upgrade existing facilities without significant expansion (Draft_NPPF_December_2025, TR5:1b).

per_question.question: According to the City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report (January 2016), why was Option A moved away from and Option B identified as the most appropriate for the city centre?
per_question.answer:
Option A was moved away from because it represents a non-viable or achievable alternative due to changing retail patterns raising concerns about the full extent of retail needs over the long term and the viability of solely retail-led regeneration (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Paragraph 5.12). 
Option B has been identified as the most appropriate as it maintains an appropriate balance and platform from which to focus the city centre's retail core (City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Paragraph 5.12).

References:
- City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016, Paragraph 5.12 (Source 1)
contexts: mixed developments and active frontages with a focused element to link uses and art with their surroundings – e.g. Swanswell and Civic Quarters. However, from the evidence of the scoring, this option does not meet the challenges that have emerged since 2001 and scored negatively in respect of the socio-economic objectives mainly due to the fact policies for the city centre developed 15 years ago do not meet the challenges facing the city centre up to 2031. City Centre Area Action Plan – Proposed Submission Sustainability Appraisal Report, January 2016 Page 24 of 104 Reasons for Rejecting Alternative Options 5.9 The results of a SA may reveal that there is no single, best performing option. Where there is no obvious discernible difference at a strategic scale, the SA process will record this as an outcome for that particular stage of the assessment process. Whilst SA informs plan making and selection of polices, the local authority is not obliged to carry forward the most sustainable options if they have reason to prefer an alternative option. 5.10 One of the overriding strategic issues that have become apparent throughout the SA/SEA process is the spatial pattern of growth, regeneration and site redevelopment and associated reasonable alternative options are massively constrained by the city's ring road. In terms of appraising the options and how areas of land are considered for potential future development, it is clear from the CCAAP, that the environmental constraints have been considered and applied. 5.11 The Council’s suite of evidence base reports provide a clear understanding of many areas that are constrained by several environmental assets including, Flood Zones 3 and 2, listed buildings, conservation area status and potential effects on views and vistas, which have placed further restrictions on where land could be considered for intervention within the city centre. 5.12 Changing retail patterns have raised concerns about the full extent of retail needs over the long term and the viability of solely retail led regeneration. Therefore option A has been moved away from as it represents a non-viable or achievable alternative. per_question.question: According to the Coventry Planning Document, which site references (e.g., NB6B, NB7B, NB8B) are identified as preventing the merging of towns, and which towns are specified?
per_question.answer:
The site references identified as preventing the merging of towns are NB6B, NB7B, and NB8B (Coventry Planning Document, Appendix_3_-_PPG2_Purposes_Analysis.pdf, Schedule 3: Nuneaton and Bedworth). 
NB6B prevents Bulkington and Nuneaton from merging (Coventry Planning Document, Appendix_3_-_PPG2_Purposes_Analysis.pdf, Schedule 3: Nuneaton and Bedworth). 
NB7B prevents Bedworth and Nuneaton from merging (Coventry Planning Document, Appendix_3_-_PPG2_Purposes_Analysis.pdf, Schedule 3: Nuneaton and Bedworth). 
NB8B prevents Nuneaton and Burton Hastings from merging (Coventry Planning Document, Appendix_3_-_PPG2_Purposes_Analysis.pdf, Schedule 3: Nuneaton and Bedworth). 
The towns specified are Bulkington, Nuneaton, Bedworth, and Burton Hastings (Coventry Planning Document, Appendix_3_-_PPG2_Purposes_Analysis.pdf, Schedule 3: Nuneaton and Bedworth).

per_question.question: According to the draft Air Quality SPD for Coventry, what assessments are major developments required to undertake, and in what circumstances might smaller developments also require assessments?
per_question.answer:
All major developments will be required to undertake full air quality assessments (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, paragraph 1.5). Where appropriate, exposure assessments will also apply to smaller developments in accordance with the guidance (Cabinet_Member_Report_air_quality_SPD_final_draft_10_Dec_2018, paragraph 1.5).

The LETCP seeks to promote joint working to reduce regulated road transport emissions, primarily Oxides of Nitrogen (NOx) and particulates (as coarse, PM10 and fine, PM2.5, fractions). Building on policies and measures designed to encourage a shift to sustainable transport modes, the LETCP seeks to target emission improvements of buses and taxis through the accelerated take-up of cleaner fuels and technologies and by discouraging the use of high emission vehicles. 1.5 The impacts of poor air quality can extend across local authority boundaries. To enable a consistent approach to implementation across Coventry and its neighbouring areas, the draft Air Quality SPD has been developed in partnership with the Coventry and Warwickshire authorities. This has included representatives from planning, environmental health and public health which has enabled important contributions from these specialist service areas. To support the improvement in the city’s air quality the revised draft SPD should be applied in conjunction with the Low Emissions Strategy and Good Practice Guidance on Planning and Procurement for the West Midlands (2014) developed by the LETCP. per_question.question: According to Appendix E of the SFRA (HZG-JBAU-XX-XX-RP-HM-0008-A1-C03), which roads and properties in the northwest end of Allesley are located within Flood Zones 2 and 3 along the River Sherbourne?
per_question.answer:
The extent of Flood Zone 2 along the River Sherbourne begins just upstream of Pikers Lane, however, the flood extent is limited to local roads and a couple of isolated buildings until the watercourse reaches Streamside Close, in the northwest end of Allesley, where the Flood Zone 3 extent begins (HZG-JBAU-XX-XX-RP-HM-0008-A1-C03-SFRA_AppendixE_FloodRiskSummary_Coventry, Appendix E). 
There are several properties along Washbrook Lane and Butt Lane located in Flood Zones 2 and 3 (HZG-JBAU-XX-XX-RP-HM-0008-A1-C03-SFRA_AppendixE_FloodRiskSummary_Coventry, Appendix E).

Surface water in the area follows the topography, predominantly flowing downhill from the higher areas in the north and west of the area mainly following the path of the main watercourses and their tributaries and roads in the area. There are also many small isolated areas of surface water ponding throughout the residential areas, which may present a localised flood risk to properties. In general, a lot of the areas of surface water risk correlate with those of fluvial risk, however, there are additional flow paths flowing downhill towards the River Sherbourne alongside flow paths along roads in the area and isolated areas of surface water ponding. The surface water flood risk following the path of the watercourses in the area also typically shows a wider flood extent than the fluvial flood outline. per_question.question: According to the MOU referenced in the Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report October 2017, how many dwellings are to be delivered in NBBC, and how does this compare to the housing figure in NBBC’s draft plan?
per_question.answer:
According to the MOU referenced in the Coventry Local Plan Inspector’s Report October 2017, 14,060 dwellings are to be delivered in NBBC (Coventry Local Plan, Inspector’s Report October 2017, paragraph 61). per_question.question: According to the Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, how was the Sustainability Appraisal of the Local Plan Proposed Modifications carried out?
per_question.answer:
The Sustainability Appraisal of the Local Plan Proposed Modifications was carried out by Council officers in workshops (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Section 3.2). Guidance was provided and care was taken to ensure high levels of consistency (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Section 3.2). The appraisal group had a wide range of specialist technical knowledge to rigorously assess potential impacts against the sustainability objectives (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Section 3.3). The appraisal was carried out in line with national guidance (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Section 3.3). A mix of expertise was sought when selecting members of the appraisal group, which included experience in property development, climate change, regeneration, planning, urban design, conservation, archaeology, and housing strategy (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017 Sustainability Appraisal/Strategic Environmental Assessment Addendum Report, Section 4.3).

per_question.question: According to Policy GE1 Green Infrastructure in the Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017, what must new development proposals do regarding green infrastructure?
per_question.answer:
According to Policy GE1 Green Infrastructure in the Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017, new development proposals should make provision for green infrastructure to ensure that such development is integrated into the landscape and contributes to improvements in connectivity and public access, biodiversity, landscape conservation, design, archaeology and recreation (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017, Policy GE1, point 2). 
New development will be expected to maintain the quantity, quality and functionality of existing green infrastructure (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017, Policy GE1, point 4). 
Where quantity is not retained, enhancement to quality is expected (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017, Policy GE1, point 4). 
Coventry's existing and planned network of green infrastructure should be used as a way of adapting to climate change through the management and enhancement of existing habitats (Coventry Local Plan – Proposed Modifications, March 2017, Policy GE1, point 3).

per_question.question: According to the Supplementary Planning Document, what is the SPD's stance on the replication of traditional Ancient Arden design elements in new developments as stated on page 7?
per_question.answer:
According to the Supplementary Planning Document, on page 7, it is stated that "There is no fundamental expectation that these will be replicated verbatim across new developments, however these are intended to provide a helpful reference for how the more traditional elements of Ancient Arden design can be incorporated and interpreted within new development proposals" (Appendix_2___Consultation_Statement___SUE_Design_Guidance, page 7). The SPD's stance is that traditional Ancient Arden design elements should be incorporated and interpreted within new developments, but not replicated verbatim (Appendix_2___Consultation_Statement___SUE_Design_Guidance, page 7).
